title: for Loop Variations: Different Update Steps
learningObjectives: Use different update expressions to control how a for-loop counter changes.
Predict sequences produced by positive and negative step sizes.
Select an update step that matches a counting pattern.
Trace a loop that updates more than one variable in its header.
Recognize how mismatched conditions and updates can cause skipped iterations or nontermination.

understand.concept: A for loop does not have to increase its counter by exactly one. Its update expression can add a larger amount, subtract an amount, or update multiple variables. The condition must agree with the starting value and update direction so the loop reaches its stopping point.
understand.whyItMatters: Step size expresses patterns such as every second number, countdowns, or regular intervals. Matching the update to the condition helps avoid skipped values or endless loops.
understand.analogy: Imagine walking along marked floor tiles. You can move one tile, two tiles, or step backward—but your direction and stopping rule must match the plan.
understand.analogyLimit: The update expression can do more than move a counter. It may update multiple variables or use an expression that is not a simple arithmetic step.

explain.narrative: The third expression in a for-loop header runs after each body execution. It can be n += 3, n -= 2, or a comma-separated sequence such as left++, right--. Use an increasing counter with an increasing condition, or a decreasing counter with a decreasing condition. If the update moves away from the condition's stopping point, the loop may never end. Trace actual values instead of assuming a step of one.

examples.title: Increase by three
examples.explanation: Each update adds three, producing 1, 4, 7, and 10.

examples.title: Count down by two
examples.explanation: The counter decreases by two, and the condition allows the final odd value 1.

examples.title: Visit every fourth value
examples.explanation: The exclusive boundary means 16 is not printed; values below it are visited in steps of four.

examples.title: Update two counters
examples.code: for (let left = 0, right = 5; left < 3; left++, right--) {\n  console.log(left + ':' + right);\n}
examples.explanation: Both update expressions run after each iteration: left increases while right decreases.

examples.title: A step that crosses the boundary
examples.explanation: After printing 9, n becomes 13 and the condition becomes false. The loop does not need to land on 10.

commonMistakes: Assuming every for loop uses i++.
Using a decreasing update with an increasing condition, or vice versa.
Expecting a step to land exactly on the boundary when the condition can stop after crossing it.
Changing the same counter in both the body and update header without tracing it.
Using a step that skips values needed for the intended sequence.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Print multiples of five
guidedTask.instructions: Use a for loop to print 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25.
steps: Increase the counter by 5 each time.
Print the counter in the body.
Trace the next value after 25 to confirm termination.
guidedTask.starterCode: for (let multiple = 5; multiple <= 25; multiple += 5) {\n  // print the multiple\n}

independentTask.title: Independent: Two counters moving together
independentTask.instructions: Write a for loop that prints five lines. One counter should show 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 while another shows 20, 17, 14, 11, 8.
requirements: Declare both counters in the initialization section.
Use one condition that controls exactly five iterations.
Print both values each iteration and explain the update section.

hints: The update section runs after the body, before the next condition check.
Use += to add a step larger than one.
Make the condition agree with the counter's direction.
A loop can update more than one variable with comma-separated expressions.
Trace the counter sequence to check the intended number of iterations.

questions.prompt: What does n += 3 do in a for-loop update?
questions.explanation: The += operator adds the right-hand amount to the current value.

questions.prompt: Which header counts down from 12 to 4 by two?
questions.explanation: The start is high, the condition allows values down to 4, and the update subtracts two.

questions.prompt: What values are printed by for (let n = 2; n < 11; n += 4)?
questions.explanation: The loop adds four and stops when n becomes 14, which is not less than 11.

questions.prompt: Can the update section of a for loop change two variables?
options: No, only one variable is allowed
Only if the loop condition is omitted
questions.explanation: A for header can update multiple variables after each body execution.

questions.prompt: Which change is most likely to make a countdown loop terminate correctly?
options: Keep n >= 1 and change n++ to n--
Keep n-- but change n >= 1 to n < 1
Start n at 1 and keep n >= 1 with n--
questions.answer: Keep n >= 1 and change n++ to n--
questions.explanation: A decreasing counter starting above the boundary moves toward a condition that eventually becomes false.
